question: Across all 28,097 live trades the average is -0.125R after costs, and only 3 of 33 sessions were green in aggregate (mean -106R/day, worst -458R on 11-17). Is the system-wide daily R in weeks 5-7 any better than in weeks 1-2, once you hold the setup mix fixed? If not, what concrete evidence says the effort is converging rather than churning?
why_it_matters: Seven weeks and ~850 trades a day should show a trend. If the aggregate curve is flat or getting worse, the process of finding, promoting and demoting setups is not adding value, however busy it looks.

answer.short_answer: Partly. Holding the setup mix fixed, R per trade got slightly less bad: on the 77 setups that traded in both weeks 1-2 and weeks 5-7, weighted by their weeks 1-2 volume, it went from -0.169 to -0.113. That gain is small and not statistically significant (t about 1.1, slope about +0.001R per session). It also mostly disappears if week 3 is counted as "early" (-0.117 to -0.112). Total daily R got worse, from -76 to -145 R/day, because trades per day roughly doubled and every new setup added since then also loses (-0.14R/trade). The most important point: a setup's live rank in the first half does not predict its rank in the second half (Spearman -0.11 across 58 setups). So promoting and demoting setups on live results has not yet shown any skill. The process is churning more than it is converging. What can be salvaged is a slow, real improvement in loss per trade inside fixed setups, and the fact that losses are spread out rather than structural, though even 0.0R/trade would still not be a profit.

answer.improvement: Set up a pre-registered convergence test that runs before any further promotions. Freeze a fixed panel of about 50 setups, with no rule edits, for 10 sessions. Each Friday, compute (a) that panel's avg R/trade and (b) the out-of-sample rank correlation between each setup's live record up to week k and its record in week k+1. Add a third measure, (c) the second-half R of the leaders chosen by the current selection rule versus random picks of the same size. Use shrunk scores, at least 30 trades and at least 15 active days. Treat the process as converging only when (b) is reliably above 0 and (c) beats random after costs. Until then, stop adding volume: growth in trades per day is the main reason total daily R is getting worse.

question: Live winners average +0.59R and losers -0.91R with a 52% win rate. Why are losses close to a full 1R while winners are capped well under 1R? Is it the targets, time stops or EOD flattening, or the giveback found in giveback_1119? And what would the expectancy be if the median winner reached 1.0R?
why_it_matters: For an intraday pro this one number explains most of the bleed. The fix may be an exit-structure problem common to all setups, not a reason to keep finding new entries.

answer.short_answer: Mostly it is the target design, plus costs and slippage on stops. Giveback, time stops and EOD flattening are a smaller part. Most setups are built 0.5R target / 1R stop (t05s1 is 71% of the 2-year lab trades), so the median winner of +0.48R is that 0.5R target being hit. Losses run past 1R because stops fill with slippage and costs on top: the median loser is -1.06R, and the 9,422 trades that lost more than 1R gave up 1,170R beyond the stop, a third of the 3,500R total live loss. If the median winner reached 1.0R with the same win rate, expectancy would go from -0.125R to about +0.21R. That 'same win rate' assumption is the catch: giveback_1119 tested 3,836 exit/target/trail/lock configs and none passed, and further targets lost R in every case, because a further target cuts the hit rate about as much as it raises the payoff.
evidence: live_trades.pkl (28,097 trades, r after costs, 10-06..11-19): win rate 52.3%, avg win +0.586R, median win +0.478R, avg loss -0.903R, median loss -1.057R, expectancy -0.125R/trade, total -3,500R. (giveback_1119 REPORT says -0.151R on the LR8 basis, so the pkl's cost basis differs slightly.)

Winner percentiles p25/p50/p75/p90 = 0.30/0.48/0.78/1.08R. Only 7.7% of all trades finish at or above +0.95R and 1.0% at or above +1.9R. Loser p10/p50 = -1.20/-1.06R. 34% of all trades end at or below -0.95R, and 25% below -1.05R.

question: 27,228 generator specs were screened plus 1,109 backlog ideas. How many configurations in total have touched the locked holdouts or the live record? Does the sqrt(2 ln N) bar use the true cumulative N across all research folders, or a per-study N?
why_it_matters: If N is counted per study, the significance bar is far too low. The 10 'positive' survivors are then about what pure noise would produce.

answer.short_answer: The sqrt(2 ln N) bar uses N per lineage, or in practice per study. It never uses the cumulative N across all research. The rules say this outright (RESEARCH_RULES rules 19, 22, 30, 33: "N = configurations tried in the lineage"), and scripts hard-code N_STUDY or N_LINEAGE values such as 9, 12, 15 and 200. Counted across the whole program, N is roughly 20 million configurations, which puts the bar near t 5.8 instead of the usual 1.5-3.7. No live setup gets close to that; the best is t 3.50. Generator setups (27,228 specs, 90 live) face no t-bar at all. The live record does somewhat better than pure noise (about 1 clear outlier out of 142), but the 10 'positive survivors' are mostly what selection plus a few big days would produce. The one candidate worth saving is NM-ETF-late-dip: t 3.50 over 15 days, and its best day is only 21% of its R. That clears the live-only bar for N=220 (3.28) but not a program-wide bar.

question: Of 142 setups with 20+ live trades, 29 have positive avg R and 10 stay positive without their best day. How does that compare with 142 random-entry setups of the same trade counts, same costs and same stops? Has anyone run that live-equivalent null?
why_it_matters: If random entries give 10/142 'survivors' too, the system has no edge yet. Every promotion decision would then be selecting noise.

answer.short_answer: Nobody has run a live-equivalent random-entry null. Random-entry controls exist only inside individual backtests (RESEARCH_RULES rule 22, ULT-13/15/17). They have never been run against the live leaderboard. I ran statistical nulls on the 28,097 live trades (R after costs). The fairest one keeps each setup's own payoff shape, stops and day clustering but gives every setup the same pool-average edge. Under that null you expect about 13 'survivors' out of 142, against 10 observed, so the survivor count is no better than noise. Weaker shuffle nulls, which ignore each setup's payoff shape, give about 5. Against those, 10 looks like a 3-4% tail result, but that test overstates it. Bottom line: at portfolio level the live record cannot yet be told apart from 'all setups equally bad', so promotions based on 'positive without best day' are mostly picking noise. The pool as a whole runs at -0.125R per trade. That is worse than the -0.02 to -0.06R that backtested random entries lose in the research files, though that comparison is not like-for-like.
evidence: Search: no portfolio/live null in docs/, mcf/, research/ledger.jsonl or the 1119/1120 folders. Random-entry controls appear only per study (docs/RESEARCH_RULES.md rule 22 'beats random entries'; mcf/research/arena/screen.py; research/ultimate_1119/round2/ULT-13, ULT-15, ULT-17 RESULTS.md).

Reproduced the setup_stats.pkl figures exactly (max diff 2e-16). Observed n>=20: 142 setups, 29 with avg R > 0, 10 that also stay positive without their best day, 7 of those 10 with best-day share >= 50%.
Pool mean -0.1246 R/trade. Mean of setup averages (n>=20) -0.138, median -0.134.
Null A, global label shuffle (300 reps): positives 13.9 [5-95%: 9-19]; survivors 5.3 [2-9]; P(>=10 survivors) = 0.04.
Null B, shuffle within each date (keeps each setup's dates and market-day effect): positives 14.7 [9-20]; survivors 5.5 [2-9]; P(>=10) = 0.03.

Null D, each setup's own trades re-centred to the pool mean -0.125, whole days resampled (keeps stop/target geometry, fat tails and day clustering): positives 23.7 [17-31], P(>=29) = 0.12; survivors 13.1 [8-19], P(>=10) = 0.83. This is the closest stand-in for 'same counts, same costs, same stops, no edge'.

Null C, same as D but re-centred to -0.05 (the random-entry loss level in the research files): survivors 26.5 [19-35]. If setups were even as good as backtested random entries, about 26 would survive, not 10.
A and B put 29 positives far in the tail (P = 0) while D does not. The spread comes from differing payoff shapes (skewed long-target versus tight-stop setups), not from skill.

For each live setup, replay the same symbols, sessions, entry minutes (within ±30 min), side, stop/target geometry, the LR8 cost model and the same trade count, with random entry bars, 200+ reps, from stored minute bars (not MarcoFlow, not the locked block). Report each setup's avg R minus its matched-random avg R, plus the portfolio count of survivors against the null distribution. Promote only on that difference, not on raw positive-without-best-day. question: With trade-R std around 0.87 and edges of +0.1-0.2R, about 75-300 independent trades per setup are needed to reach t≈2, and trades on the same day are correlated. At current rep rates, how many sessions until each Testing setup reaches a verdict? How many of the 215 enabled setups can realistically get one in the next quarter?
why_it_matters: If most setups can never reach a verdict, running 215 at once spreads exposure across setups that will never resolve.

answer.short_answer: Mostly yes. At current rates, a typical Testing setup needs about 146 more active sessions to prove a +0.15R edge at t≈2 once same-day correlation is counted. That is roughly 7 months. In the next quarter (about 63 sessions), only 22 of the 101 Testing A/B/D/E/F setups (51 of all 217 enabled) can confirm a +0.15R edge. For a +0.1R edge it is 1 of 101 (10 of 217). A larger +0.2R edge could be confirmed by 42 of 101 (106 of 217). The useful side is that negative verdicts come much faster: 23 enabled setups already have a clustered 95% upper bound below 0 and 49 below +0.1R. The system can therefore resolve losers within the quarter and free slots for setups that trade more often. The house bar of 15 active days and 30 trades does not settle anything: at 30 trades the clustered standard error is about 0.18R, so it can only detect edges of roughly ±0.35R.

question: Why run 215 enabled setups across 10 accounts rather than putting the same capital and attention on the top 20? What is the marginal information gained per added setup, given 69 have fewer than 20 trades and 25 have zero?
why_it_matters: Breadth without reps dilutes power. A pro would concentrate on the few candidates with a real thesis.

answer.short_answer: The concern is partly right, but the reason is not quite the one the outsider gives. The thin setups cost almost nothing: the 78 setups with fewer than 20 trades took only 562 of 28,097 trades (2%) and -31.8R in total. Narrowing to a "top 20" would not have fixed the results either. When setups were ranked on earlier sessions, those rankings did not predict later results (Spearman -0.06 and -0.12), and the 20 best on paper still lost money afterwards (-0.08R and -0.06R per trade, against about -0.12R for everything else). The real waste is the many setups that have plenty of trades and keep losing: setups with 20+ trades made -3,843R from the losers against +375R from the winners. The Graveyard alone took 35% of all trades for -1,177R. So the bottleneck is finding an edge, not how widely the effort is spread. question: Backtest top-10 medians are negative, yet live performance is also negative. For each live setup, what is the mean live-minus-backtest R per trade over the same dates, and does the gap come mostly from entry fills, stop fills or exits? Is the backtester trusted for anything at this point?

answer.short_answer: First, a correction to the question: for the top-10 setups, live results are positive and the 2-year backtest is negative. Over the same dates (10-06..11-04), the backtest also reads below live. Live minus backtest is about +0.09R per trade weighted by trades (simple mean +0.076R, median about +0.165R). 7 of the 10 setups did better live and 3 did worse (RW6 -0.35, ST7 -0.10, NM-RWN4 -0.05). Part of that gap is selection bias, because these 10 were picked for doing well live. The gap is almost all about which trades get taken, not about fills or exits. Only 40-100% of live symbol-days appear in the backtest at all. Measured execution moves the other way: fills cost live about 0.025-0.04R per trade. So entry fills, stop fills and exits do not explain the gap. We have two simulators, and they earn different trust. The session replay runs the real live runner and is trusted for fill and exit mechanics: on trades it matches with live, it is off by +0.005R per trade. It is not trusted for picking which trades happen: it matches 87% of live trades and adds 26% extra trades, so it currently counts 0 toward promotion. The 2-year lab backtester has not predicted the live winners. Its "REALLY BAD" rule would reject the live #1 (L3-fromopen). question: How do Alpaca paper fills compare with what a real account would get on low-float, extended-tier and leveraged-ETF names (SOXL, SOXS, APLD are the most traded)? Has the cost model in mcf/costs.py been checked against real fills, or only against paper?
why_it_matters: Paper fills are usually optimistic on stops and fast names. An edge of -0.12R on paper could be clearly worse with real money.

answer.short_answer: Only against paper. mcf/costs.py (the LR8 cost model, used from 11-12) was calibrated by comparing Alpaca paper fills with 1-minute SIP bars on 4 sessions. MCF has never placed a real-money trade, so no real fill has ever been compared, and the tick-level quote check (LR15/LR6-D) is not recorded as done. Stops are not where paper flatters. Paper stop fills were already 4.6 bps beyond the stop, and 28% were worse than every print in their minute. The optimism is in profit-target (limit) exits. LR8 removes the price improvement there, but its base model does not charge for the 11% of target fills that only touched the price, a further ~0.035R per trade. SOXL, SOXS and APLD are only 1.3% of trades, and their slippage was never measured on its own. So real money would most likely run about 0.03-0.05R worse than today's cost-in figure. At an all-trade average of -0.125R, that would not turn the system's results around.

question: How is 1R defined: stop distance at entry, fixed dollars, or ATR? Did that definition or the sizing rule change inside the 7-week window? Is R comparable between a 5-cent stop on a $3 stock and a $2 stop on DELL?
why_it_matters: If R is not stable or comparable, summing R across setups and across rule changes mixes apples and oranges, and the leaderboard is misleading.

answer.short_answer: 1R is each trade's own stop distance at entry: shares x |entry - stop|. It is not fixed dollars and not ATR. Trade R is P/L after costs divided by that risk. That definition has stayed the same for the whole window, but three things around it changed. The dollar size of a trade changed several times, because the slot (capital per position) cap sets size on nearly every trade, not the 0.25% risk budget. The cost basis behind 'R after costs' changed on 11-11 and 11-12. And from 11-20, stop prices round to the cent away from price. So R works as a unit for judging a setup, but it does not convert to dollars: a 5-cent stop on a $3 stock and a $2 stop on DELL each count as 1R while risking very different dollar amounts, and the tight stop pays far more cost per R.

Trade R = pnl / (shares x stop distance) (mcf/execution/reconcile.py:113, shadow.py:766); after costs = pnl_adj / risk (ledger LR2, 11-11).

The slot cap sets trade size on ~every lot (research/sizing_1116/NOTES.md:28; config/account_*.yaml comments). Trades rarely risk the nominal 0.25% of equity, so the dollars behind 1R vary from trade to trade with stop width and price.

question: Today 10 textbook setups were 0/10 profitable after costs, yet 2 were admitted to testing because they 'meet the top-10 standard'. If that standard admits setups that lose on the check, what is it actually filtering? Should the bar be 'positive after costs on the history', full stop?

answer.short_answer: The concern is partly right. The top-10 standard is a relative bar, not a profit bar. It admits anything that backtests no worse than MCF's live winners do, and those winners backtest negative too (Tier A wants T1 combined >= -0.038R and CHECK >= -0.046R). So it screens out the clearly bad ones (6 of 10 beginner setups failed, most marked REALLY BAD). It does not pick out real edge: BEG-01 stopOR scores -0.026R on CHECK against -0.032R for random entries, and BEG-03 rests on one day. But "positive after costs on the history, full stop" would not fix this. It would have rejected the best live setup, L3-fromopen (+0.204R over 397 live trades; backtest -0.085R). The generator setups, which all had to be positive on both train and valid history, are doing worse live than the hand-built ones. The backtest sign predicts live poorly whichever way the bar is set, so the stronger filter is edge against random entries and gross edge larger than costs, not the sign of the backtest.

question: Entries are triggered on 1-minute bars. What is the median delay from signal bar close to fill, and how much does price move against the trade in that time? Have any setups been tested with stop-limit or limit entries at the trigger price instead of market at the next bar?
why_it_matters: On fast names, one bar of delay can consume much of a 0.2R edge. Execution may matter more than the choice of setup.

answer.short_answer: The delay is short, and slippage costs a few hundredths of an R per trade, not most of the edge. Across 20,849 live entries from 10-12 to 11-12, the runner sends its order a median 34 s after the 1-minute signal bar closes (it polls once a minute). Alpaca fills a median 1.6 s after that, so about 36 s from bar close to fill. Median adverse move is 3.7 bps, or +0.04R. The mean is +0.022R once 177 outliers beyond ±1R are dropped, and 63% of entries fill worse than the signal price. Every live R figure is already measured from the actual fill, so this cost is inside all reported results. It does not explain why most setups lose: if every trade had filled at the signal price, setups with 20+ trades that are positive would rise only from 28 to 36 of 119. Limit entries have been tested once, on one setup. The 10-13 study gave the 09:45 dip a passive limit and it failed: 0 of 957 configurations passed. No live setup uses stop-limit entries. Stop-entry signals become a market order when the trigger trades.

question: What protections exist against runaway behavior: a daily loss limit per account and system-wide, a max open positions limit, a check for stuck orders, duplicate order prevention? Did any of them trigger on 11-17 (-458R, 1,552 trades)?
why_it_matters: An autonomous system with ~1,000+ trades a day and no hard brakes is a disaster waiting for real money.

answer.short_answer: Most of the brakes exist, but each one works inside a single account. There is no automatic loss limit across the whole system, and the account limits outside Primary are set so loose that they only catch a disaster. On 11-17, three brakes fired: the Graveyard account's 120R daily stop at about 10:50 (1,532 entries blocked), the Graveyard's -2R per-setup stop (447 blocked), and Primary's -2R per-setup stop (21 blocked). Nothing else fired: no kill switch, no watchdog flatten, no stale-data or position-mismatch event, no trade-count cap. The Generator account lost -128.7R, -134.6R of it from one setup in 144 trades, and nothing stopped it, because Gen has no per-setup stop and its account stop is 300R. Even the Graveyard, after its halt, closed at -177R after costs: the halt only stops new entries, it counts R before costs, and up to 300 open positions keep running to their exits.

Per-setup daily stop: max_setup_daily_loss_r = 2R in Primary and Graveyard, latched for the day. It is null (off) in Gen and every Testing account (ST-A 10-22 and the account yamls).

question: At real-world size (say a $50k account with 1% risk per trade), how many of the ~850 daily signals could actually be taken at once given buying power and PDT rules? Is per-setup R measured in a way that would survive those capital limits?
why_it_matters: Paper accounts with unlimited parallel trades can't be reproduced live. The real system would be a heavily filtered subset with different stats.

answer.short_answer: Very few of them. I replayed the live journals first-come on one $50k account at 1% risk with 4x intraday buying power (PDT no longer applies: FINRA retired it 2026-06-04 and Alpaca now uses intraday margin). That account could take about 25 trades a day out of roughly 850, or 3% of signals. Trading Primary's setups alone, it could take about 12 a day, 28% of Primary's signals. With a stop near 1%, 1% risk means each position is about the size of the whole account, so at most about 4 can be open at once. Per-trade R is measured independently of size, so that part carries over. Per-setup R does not: it comes from roughly $900 paper positions, with about 280 open at the same time across 10 paper accounts, paper fills and no market impact. A capped real account would trade a different, first-come subset. question: For setups with 20+ trades, does R over the last 10 trades predict the next 10 trades out of sample, or is it noise? Are promotions and demotions driven by short recent streaks?
why_it_matters: If recent form does not predict future form, moves based on it just churn the assignments without improving results.

answer.short_answer: Measured across sessions, it is noise. For the 132 setups with 20+ trades, a setup's last 10 trades at one session's close do not predict its next 10 trades on later sessions (r = -0.01, setup-clustered 95% CI -0.09 to +0.06). Hot setups (last-10 avg >= +0.5R) go on to average -0.135R, about the same as everyone else at -0.145R. The strong "persistence" you get from splitting trades into consecutive blocks of 10 (r = 0.35) comes from trades within the same day: 93% of those block boundaries fall inside one session, so it measures the day's market conditions, not the setup's form. The written rules mostly do not act on short streaks: promotion (C3-BAR2) needs 30+ trades, 15+ active days, a shrunk estimate and no reliance on one day, and the arena exit needs 30 trades, 15 days and a day-clustered t <= -1.5. Two exceptions lean on recent results: Primary demotion at -10R since admission, and the Graveyard condition "last 10 sessions <= 0". A more sobering finding: a setup's whole record to date predicts its next 10 no better (r = -0.02), so at current sample sizes ranking setups on their live record has almost no out-of-sample skill.

Scripts: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/9c6fc50d-b94d-5471-ba1f-4c82eb058810/scratchpad/outsider_scratch/q32.py (blocks of 10) and /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/9c6fc50d-b94d-5471-ba1f-4c82eb058810/scratchpad/outsider_scratch/q32b.py (split at session close). Trades are ordered by date, then by row order in the file.

Decision-relevant test (q32b), splitting at each session close: 1,599 observations across 132 setups. Last-10 avg R vs avg R of the next 10 trades on later days: Pearson -0.014 (p=0.57), Spearman -0.020; setup-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [-0.087, +0.064]. Keeping only each setup's most recent split (n=132): r = 0.004.
Next-10 avg R by last-10 quintile (worst to best): -0.149, -0.126, -0.148, -0.128, -0.173. Share of next-10 blocks that are positive: 42%, 45%, 39%, 44%, 38%. The pattern is flat.
Hot streaks: last-10 >= +0.2R (n=372) gives next-10 -0.152R; last-10 >= +0.5R (n=111) gives -0.135R. Baseline for all observations: -0.145R, 42% positive.
Whole record to date vs next 10: r = -0.016 (CI [-0.098, +0.053]). Regressing next-10 on whole record and last-10 together: coefficients -0.023 and -0.010, intercept -0.148. Neither adds anything.
It holds whether the last 10 came from a single day (n=735, r=-0.04) or were spread over 3+ days (n=464, r=-0.02).

Same-day effect (q32): 2,548 consecutive 10-trade block pairs across 142 setups give r=0.35 (Spearman 0.33). Top-quintile previous block (+0.54R) is followed by +0.097R; bottom quintile (-0.85R) by -0.37R. Removing setup averages leaves r=0.29. But the 169 pairs whose boundary falls between sessions give r = -0.19 (p=0.013), so the persistence is a same-day effect.
Noise scale: trade R standard deviation is 0.87, so the standard error of a 10-trade mean is about 0.28R. The spread of last-10 means across setups is 0.50R, much of it sampling noise.

answer.short_answer: Partly. MCF fixed the mechanical failures that sank MarcoFlow: data latency, fake fills, duplicate orders, and costs left out. It is repeating the strategic ones at roughly ten times the volume. It has too many setups (220 have traded live, 23-63 new each week), heavy rule churn (236 ledger entries in 7 weeks, 11 of them flagged mid-session) and a selection process that fits the past and then loses live (10 of 142 setups positive, 1 statistically solid). The overall result looks like MarcoFlow's: about -0.125R per trade after costs, 28,097 trades, -3,500R, and no week positive. MCF did write explicit rules against each failure mode. The rules came after the losses, though, and they have not yet turned results around.
evidence: MarcoFlow baseline (MARCOFLOW_CONTEXT.md lines 16-19): 2,123 clean trades, -$3,242, win rate 31.8%. Win rate fell with each config era (38.5 -> 42.9 -> 26.6 -> 24.5%), so rule churn there went with decay.

No week is positive and there is no upward trend. Win rate is 49-56%, higher than MarcoFlow's 32%. The losses now come from small winners against full-size losers, not from bad fills.

Too many setups is repeating. Setups trading each week went 23 -> 77 -> 93 -> 146 -> 168 -> 165 -> 173. New setups by first-trade week: 23, 63, 23, 54, 24, 10, 23. 220 have traded in total. Of the 142 with 20+ trades, only 10 have wo_avg_r > 0 and only 1 has day-clustered t >= 2 (setup_stats.pkl). That count is close to what multiple testing alone predicts.

Rule churn is repeating. research/ledger.jsonl has 236 entries with effective dates from 10-06 to 11-23. Burst days: 10-12 (23), 10-21 (15), 11-12 (17), 11-17 (29), 11-19 (27). 11 entries carry mid_session=true. Kinds include trading 61, move 30, process 26, setup 20 and risk 14. Every weekly figure above therefore spans rule changes: the cost re-basing on 11-12 (pre-11-12 rows re-costed about -0.04R each under LR8, RESEARCH_RULES rule 32), the account restructure on 11-12, the rotation/footrace from 11-20, and the C3 epoch 1 from 11-19.

Paper-fill optimism is largely addressed. Costs are always on (RESEARCH_RULES rule 1: per-share and bps slippage, extra stop slippage, 3x on extended-tier names, next-bar entries, stop checked first inside a bar). The measured fill drag is +0.041R per lot worse than the signal across 1,441 Primary lots (rule 32), far smaller than MarcoFlow's ~0.25% per trade. They look like re-entries or partial fills, not MarcoFlow's -$1,095 race. 55 setup/symbol/day cases traded in more than one account.

question: The charter's core job is to identify big movers beforehand. Of each day's top 50 movers (long and short), what share did any MCF setup trade, and with what R? Is a pre-market 'mover predictor' measured independently of setup entries?
why_it_matters: If the system rarely touches the day's real movers, the problem is selection upstream, not setup tuning. That changes where effort should go.

answer.short_answer: Move Hunt does measure capture rate. Over 14 scored sessions (10-29 to 11-19), MCF traded only 34 of the 700 top movers (4.9%) in the right direction and inside the move window, for +38.4R. On those same names it took 84 wrong-direction trades for -79.6R, so the top movers cost it about 41R net. With earnings-blackout names removed (52% of the raw list), it caught 96 of 700 (13.7%), +60.3R, against 218 wrong-direction trades at -169.5R. But it traded 64% of those tradable movers at some point that day. So the system finds the names: the misses are timing and direction ("traded outside the move" 31%, "no setup signalled" 31%, skipped for spread 14%, wrong side only 11%). That makes the outsider's 'selection upstream' framing only partly right. A pre-market mover predictor has been measured separately from setup entries, on two years of history. Its best pre-open rankings put about 2x the random share of the day's top-50 movers into a top-150 list. It is not run live, and it is not reported daily.
evidence: Source: research/bdi/moves/moves.csv (1,400 rows = 14 days x 50 movers x 2 sets) and moves_<day>_out.txt. Definition (moves.py docstring, fixed before looking): liquid names (ADV >= $95M), best 5-min decision point 09:35-15:00, move = high/low over the next 90 min in daily-ATR units, top 25 long + 25 short. 'Caught' = a live trade on the right side entered between decision-30min and the extreme. R = after-cost trade R.

Set 'all': caught 34/700 = 4.9% (long 16/350 +16.2R, short 18/350 +22.3R). Captured +38.41R total (about +1.13R per catch). Wrong-direction trades on the same names: 84 for -79.59R. Miss reasons: blackout 364, traded outside the move 116, no setup signalled 110, skipped 39, wrong side only 37. Excluding blackout names: 34/336 = 10%.

Set 'tradable' (blackout removed, list re-ranked): caught 96/700 = 13.7%, +60.33R. Wrong-direction: 218 trades for -169.47R. Any trade on the symbol that day: 447/700 = 64%. Misses: outside the move 217, no setup signalled 215, skipped 98, wrong side only 74.
Daily catches swing a lot. 'All' set: 1-5 per day. 11-17 gave +12.64R from only 2 catches and 11-12 gave +9.31R from 5. Five days caught just 1/50. Capture R is lumpy and leans on a few days.

Coverage check: the moves_1119 header shows 1,066 live trades (577 symbols). That equals all 11-19 rows in live_trades.pkl across the 10 post-restructure accounts, so the capture count is not missing new accounts.

Independent predictor: research/bdi/eu1103/preopen/movers.py + NOTES.md (2-year TRAIN/VALID, locked block asserted out). Share of the day's top-50 rest-of-day-range movers that land in the top 150 of a pre-open ranking: opening-bar $vol/adv20 38% TRAIN / 33% VALID (random 18%/15%); pre-market range 36%/33%; pre-market relative volume 34%/31%; overnight news 32%/29%; gap 33%/29%. Those are post hoc descriptive checks (17), separate from the 756 pre-declared gates. 0 of 9 pre-open gates improved the setups' R.

Precursor scans (precursors.py, e.g. precursors_1119_out.txt): vol_exp ('in play') top quintile shows 2-4x lift for big moves on both sides. But MH1 (10-29) found it predicts move size, not direction. MH1109-P1 tested the compass direction plus in-play on 11-09 and got excess -0.286R vs the base.

Production: no capture-rate or Move Hunt field shows up in mcf/report/daily_post.py, team.py or intraday.py. The capture rate lives only in research outputs, even though docs/BDI_CHARTER.md line 17 says to 'track a daily capture rate'.
answer.improvement: Move the 09:35 'on deck' mover ranking (opening-bar $vol/adv20 + pre-market range + overnight news) and the moves.py capture score into the nightly report. Then run one pre-registered study that scores setup entries only on the top-150 'on deck' names, split by miss reason. The question is whether a direction/timing rule on known movers (e.g. first pullback after the 09:35-09:45 start, side from the compass) turns the 64% 'touched that day' into right-side catches. Also log the wrong-direction R (-169R) as its own loss category, so a targeted remedy can go after it.

theme: What a pro would do tomorrow

why_it_matters: It tests whether a simple, concentrated book beats the current sprawling machine. If it does, the overhead is pure cost.

answer.short_answer: Looking back, the book wins: the 10 setups that are positive without their best day, held over the full 7 weeks, made +231.5R on 2,150 trades (+0.108R/trade after costs). Over the same period the whole machine lost -3,500R (-0.125R/trade). But those 10 were picked using the same 7 weeks, so that figure is selection bias, not a result. Run honestly, picking the top 10 on the data available at the time and then trading them forward, the book lost money at all three cut dates (-0.256, -0.138, -0.088 R/trade). That is about the same as, or worse than, the rest of the machine over the same days (-0.124, -0.121, -0.105). The 'stocks in play' and 'one exit framework' parts cannot be replayed from the live trades, and 236 rule changes in the ledger fall inside the window. So the honest answer is that a concentrated book is not shown to beat the machine yet. The part worth saving is a small L3-gap-slope / RW3-RW5 gap-down core, and the time to concentrate is after a forward test holds up.
